items.title: Sound familiar? Kawhi Leonard tied to a secret sponsorship deal with Intuit Dome scoreboard maker
items.content:
Kawhi Leonard attends a press conference July 7 where former teammate Kyle Lowry signed a one-day contract to retire as a Toronto Raptor. (Chris Young / The Canadian Press via AP) Clippers star Kawhi Leonard had a second lucrative undisclosed sponsorship agreement with a company doing business with the team, Pablo Torre reported Thursday night on his podcast.

Scoreboard manufacturer Daktronics, which built the $100 million video board at the Clippers’ Intuit Dome, hired Leonard to a multi-million dollar endorsement deal, according to Torre. The podcast host found no evidence that the All-NBA forward did any work for the company.

The details are similar to the $28 million endorsement deal Leonard had with Aspiration, a now-defunct environmental banking company that had a 23-year, $300 million sponsorship deal with Clippers. Steve Ballmer, the team’s owner, invested $60 million into Aspiration, triggering allegations that the payment to Leonard circumvented the NBA salary cap.

That deal is at the center off an ongoing, almost year-long NBA investigation. Requests on Friday for comment from Leonard’s agent and the Clippers were not immediately answered.

The salary cap limits what teams can spend on player payroll to ensure parity and prevent the wealthiest teams from outspending smaller-market teams to acquire the best players. NBA Commissioner Adam Silver has called attempts to circumvent it a “cardinal sin.”

The topic was raised on Torre’s podcast by a person identified as an “anonymous high-level source under contract for Intuit Dome.” The person alleged in an interview that the sponsorship deal was “1,000% a way to circumvent the salary cap. It was funneling money from the Clippers through Daktronics back to Kawhi.”

Read more:NBA probe of Steve Ballmer, Kawhi Leonard and Clippers at forefront after Aspiration fraud sentencing

The investigation into the Aspiration allegations has grown in scope, the Athletic reported three weeks ago. In addition to attempting to determine whether Aspiration’s payment to Leonard violated NBA salary-cap rules, the probe conducted by high-powered New York law firm Wachtell Lipton Rosen & Katz is examining Leonard’s deal with Daktronics.

If the NBA determines that a salary-cap violation occurred, the Clippers could be fined and stripped of first-round picks. Ballmer also could be penalized and Leonard’s contract could be voided. He has one year and $50.3 million left on a three-year, $149.5 million deal he signed before the 2024-25 season. 

The endorsement deal with Daktronics raised suspicion because the company doesn’t do business with the general public and doesn’t need prominent athletes or celebrities to pitch its products. 

“Daktronics was conservative to a fault for the 20+ years I was there,” a former employee told Torre. “I remember asking early on why we didn’t do more traditional advertising and promotion to increase brand recognition. I was told that since it’s B2B and not a consumer product, it

items.title: Kevin Love’s Agent Has Been In Contact With Sixers
items.content:
Jeff Schwartz, Kevin Love‘s agent at Excel Sports Management, has been in contact with the Sixers since LeBron James announced he’d be signing with the team, sources tell Dave McMenamin of ESPN.

As McMenamin writes, James and Love were teammates for several years in Cleveland and have remained close since then, vacationing together earlier this summer. However, that doesn’t necessarily mean that there will be an opportunity for Love in Philadelphia this season.

The 76ers are currently just $1.83MM away from their first-apron hard cap with 14 players on standard contracts. Adding a 15th man on a veteran’s minimum contract before the regular season would carry a $2.45MM cap hit, so it won’t be possible until December 4 – when a minimum deal has prorated down to $1.82MM – unless the team makes a roster move to generate additional space below that hard cap.

Waiving Jabari Walker, whose $2.58MM salary is only partially guaranteed for $250K, would be the easiest way to make room for a newcomer. But Walker made a positive impression on the team in a part-time role last season, averaging 4.3 points and 3.0 rebounds in 11.9 minutes per game across 64 appearances. Recent reporting has indicated that the front office would prefer to keep him.

When they needed to make room under the first apron to sign Kentavious Caldwell-Pope, the Sixers opted to attach a second-round pick to trade Johni Broome to the Clippers rather than cutting Walker, whose agent Rich Paul also represents James, Tyrese Maxey, and Justin Edwards.

Walker also just turned 24 years old last Thursday and may still have room to improve, whereas Love will turn 38 in September and has seen his production decline in recent years. Last season, the five-time All-Star averaged 6.7 PPG and 5.8 RPG in 16.6 MPG over the course of 37 appearances (five starts) for Utah, posting a shooting line of .397/.373/.841.

According to McMenamin, while Love would have interest in reuniting with James to pursue a title in Philadelphia, he also still has a strong relationship with Jazz head coach Will Hardy and was a valued veteran leader in the club’s locker room last season.

As is the case with the 76ers though, it’s unclear whether the Jazz will have room on their regular season roster for Love. Utah is currently carrying 14 players on fully guaranteed contracts, with big man Mo Bamba on a partially guaranteed deal as the potential 15th man.

items.title: Kawhi Leonard reportedly had second questionable endorsement deal with scoreboard manufacturer
items.content:
One of the things reportedly dragging out the now 11-month investigation into Kawhi Leonard's alleged "no-show" endorsement deal with Aspiration to circumvent the NBA's salary cap — which has put Leonard’s trade to Toronto on hold — was a report of a second questionable endorsement.

That second multi-million dollar endorsement deal was with South Dakota-based Daktronics, the makers of the impressive Jumbotron/Halo board inside the Inuit Dome, reports Pablo Torre on the latest edition of the “Pablo Torre Finds Out” podcast. The exact dollar value of the deal is unknown.

A source told Torre, "It was 1,000% a way to circumvent the salary cap" and that the Clippers "were technically kind of funding it." Daktronics does not have a history of celebrity endorsements, and it's unclear what, if anything, Leonard may have done for the company, but it doesn't even do traditional consumer-facing advertising. The company's PR firm told Torre, "Daktronics doesn't have a deal with Kawhi right now." It said the league had contacted it about its ongoing investigation.

Through all of this, the Clippers and owner Steve Ballmer have denied any wrongdoing and say they have nothing to hide. While they have yet to comment on this specific new allegation, here is part of the statement the Clippers gave to NBC Sports last month when the Leonard trade to Toronto was put on hold pending the conclusion of the investigation:

"For the past 10 months, our organization has fully cooperated with an NBA investigation, participating in dozens of interviews, providing tens of thousands of documents, and facilitating access to our staff."

The Daktronics angle is a second offshoot of the league's investigation into Leonard's endorsement deal with Aspiration, a former Clippers sponsor. Aspiration was a green bank company that has since gone bankrupt, and its founder, Joe Sanberg, has been convicted of defrauding investors and is spending 14 months in prison for his crimes. The law firm of Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz is conducting the investigation.

Clippers owner Ballmer was one of the investors in Aspiration. As previously pointed out on the Pablo Torre Finds Out podcast, Ballmer made a $50 million investment in Aspiration, and not long after, Leonard signed a $28 million endorsement deal with the company (he also signed a four-year, $176 million extension with the Clippers). Ballmer and the Clippers have said they introduced Leonard to Aspiration, but that was the extent of their involvement. 

The initial focus of the investigation was on that $28 million endorsement deal (which later grew to include now-worthless stock options). Multiple former Aspiration employees told Torre this was a "no-show" endorsement designed to funnel more money to Leonard and circumvent the NBA salary cap.
